examples.en: Yesterday I was reading until late at night.

note:
The Russian past tense has one form, made with the ending -л, and no auxiliary verb (nothing like «was» or «have»).

The ending shows gender and number, and a pronoun shows the person:
• я чита́л, я чита́ла - I read, I was reading (man, woman)
• ты чита́л, ты чита́ла - you read (man, woman)
• он чита́л, она́ чита́ла, оно́ чита́ло - he, she, it read
• мы, вы, они́ чита́ли - we, you, they read

So the pronoun cannot be left out: чита́л alone could mean «I read», «you read» or «he read».

There is no separate past continuous or perfect: this one form covers «I read», «I was reading» and «I have read», and aspect (чита́л, прочита́л) shows whether the action was completed.
title: The past tense: one form ending in -л

examples.en: Tomorrow I will be working all day.

related.en: I will read, I will be reading (imperfective)
I will read it through, I will finish reading (perfective)

note:
Russian has no single future ending like English «will». The future is made in two ways:

1. imperfective verb: бу́ду + infinitive - я бу́ду де́лать (I will be doing)
2. perfective verb: the present-tense form has a future meaning - я сде́лаю (I will do it, I will get it done)

A perfective verb is never used with бу́ду: «я бу́ду сде́лать» is wrong.

So «I will read it through» is я прочита́ю, and «I will be reading (for a long time, regularly)» is я бу́ду чита́ть.
title: The future: бу́ду or a perfective verb

skip: only contrasts Serbian да + present with the Russian infinitive; English also uses a plain infinitive after want, can, start

related.en: so that, in order to (also after «want», «ask»: «want you to»)

note:
When the second verb has a different subject («I want you to come», «she asks us to help»), Russian uses что́бы + the past-tense form, not an infinitive as in English.

• Хочу́, что́бы ты пришёл. - I want you to come.
• Она́ про́сит, что́бы мы помогли́. - She asks us to help.

The verb has a past-tense form, but it does not refer to the past: the action is yet to happen.

When the subject is the same, что́бы is not used: хочу́ уйти́ (I want to leave).

Что́бы also means «in order to»: Я учу́ ру́сский, что́бы свобо́дно говори́ть - I'm studying Russian in order to speak fluently.
title: что́бы: «want you to...» and «in order to»

related.en: there is, there exists (у меня есть = I have)

note:
Russian has no verb «to have» in this sense. «I have a brother» is said with «у» + gen. and «есть»:

• «У меня́ есть брат.» - I have a brother (literally: at me there is a brother).
• «У нас есть вре́мя.» - We have time.

The thing owned is the subject, and the owner is in the genitive after «у».

Negative: есть becomes нет and the thing owned goes into the genitive: «У меня́ нет бра́та» - I have no brother.

In the past, the form of быть agrees with the thing owned: «у неё была́ сестра́», «у нас бы́ло вре́мя».

The verb име́ть exists, but it sounds bookish.
title: To have: у меня́ есть and у меня́ нет

note:
After нет, не бы́ло and не бу́дет, the thing that is missing stands in the genitive, not in the nominative:

• «Здесь нет пробле́м.» - There are no problems here.
• «Вчера́ дождя́ не бы́ло.» - There was no rain yesterday.
• «В го́роде нет метро́.» - There is no metro in the city.

So it is not «нет вре́мя», but нет вре́мени.

After не with a transitive verb and a concrete object the accusative usually stays: Я не чита́ю газе́ту. The genitive is more bookish and comes with abstract nouns: не име́ет значе́ния.
title: Negation and the genitive

note:
After «become» and «work as», Russian uses the instrumental, not the nominative.

• стать врачо́м - to become a doctor
• рабо́тать инжене́ром - to work as an engineer
• быть учи́телем - to be a teacher (in the past and future: Он был учи́телем)

The instrumental also follows станови́ться, остава́ться, каза́ться, называ́ться: Он оказа́лся врачо́м - It turned out that he was a doctor.

In the present tense there is no verb, so the nominative stays: Он учи́тель.
title: To become, to be, to work as: the instrumental

examples.en: Mom is at work right now.
The children are at school until two.
I'm going to the post office.

note:
Russian has two prepositions for places, and English «in» or «at» does not tell you which one to use.

• на - рабо́та, по́чта, вокза́л, ста́нция, ры́нок, у́лица, ку́хня: на рабо́те, на по́чте, на вокза́ле
• в - шко́ла, магази́н, больни́ца, кварти́ра, го́род: в шко́ле, в магази́не, в больни́це

Motion toward a place: the same preposition + accusative: на по́чту, на рабо́ту, в шко́лу.

Common mistakes are «в по́чте» and «в рабо́те»: «at the post office» is на по́чте.

There is no rule: learn the preposition together with the word.
title: «In» or «at»: в and на with places

related.en: God! (a relic of the old vocative)

note:
Russian has no vocative case: a person is addressed in the nominative.

• Ма́ша! - Masha!
• Ми́ша, иди́ сюда́! - Misha, come here!

In conversation, names ending in «-а» and «-я» lose that ending, which gives something like a vocative: Маш! Мам! Пап! Ко́ль! Серёж!

This is only for close people and is optional. Relics of the old vocative are Бо́же! and Го́споди!
title: The vocative: Russian has none

note:
After a number the noun is in the genitive: singular after 2, 3 and 4, plural after 5 and more. English speakers expect a plain plural, so the details matter.

• два for masculine and neuter, две for feminine: два бра́та, две сестры́
• an adjective after 2-4 is in the genitive plural: два но́вых стола́, but две но́вые кни́ги
• год: два го́да, but пять лет
• пять челове́к, not «челове́ков»
• 21, 31...: оди́н at the end means the noun is singular: два́дцать оди́н стол
title: Numbers and cases: the traps after 2-4 and 5+

examples.en: He left the house at seven.
Drop by my place in the evening.

related.en: to drop by, to stop in

note:
Russian makes verbs like «to come», «to leave», «to go in», «to go out», «to cross» and «to pass» from the root -йти and a prefix: прийти́, уйти́, войти́, вы́йти, перейти́, пройти́. They are perfective.

• пришёл, пришла́ - came (m., f.)
• ушёл, ушла́ - left
• вошёл, вошла́ - went in
• вы́шел, вы́шла - went out
• перешёл, прошёл, зашёл - crossed, passed, dropped by

When you travel by vehicle: прие́хать, уе́хать, въе́хать (-е́хать instead of -йти́).
title: Came, left, went in, went out: prefixed verbs of motion

note:
Unlike мой and твой, the words его́ (his), её (her) and их (their) never change for gender or case.

• его́ сестра́, с его́ сестро́й, о его́ сестре́
• её брат, с её бра́том
• их до́ма (the form «и́хний» is heard, but it is non-standard)

Свой refers back to the subject of the sentence: Он взял свою́ ку́ртку (his own jacket). Он взял её ку́ртку - he took her jacket, someone else's.

Свой changes like мой: свой, своя́, своё, свои́.
title: свой or его́, её, их

examples.en: I'm very glad to see you.

note:
Some adjectives have a short form in the predicate: no ending in the masculine, and the gender shows in the ending.

• Я рад. - I'm glad.
• Он бо́лен, она́ больна́. - He is ill, she is ill.
• Он гото́в, она́ гото́ва. - He is ready, she is ready.
• Он до́лжен, она́ должна́. - He must, she must (is obliged to).
• Он за́нят, она́ занята́. - He is busy, she is busy.

After the masculine form the stress often moves: бо́лен, больна́, больно́, больны́. Рад changes like this: рад, ра́да, ра́до, ра́ды.

These forms are not used before a noun: there the full adjective is used.
title: Short adjectives: рад, бо́лен, гото́в, до́лжен

examples.en: This car is cheaper than that one.
She is two years older than me.

note:
In the predicate the Russian comparative does not change for gender or number and ends in -ее or -е: быстре́е, деше́вле, ста́рше.

• Э́то деше́вле. - This is cheaper.
• Сестра́ ста́рше. - My sister is older.

Comparing:
1. чем + nominative: Он ста́рше, чем я.
2. genitive without чем: Он ста́рше меня́, ста́рше бра́та.

Irregular: хоро́ший - лу́чше, плохо́й - ху́же, мно́го - бо́льше, ма́ло - ме́ньше.

«Much older» is гора́здо ста́рше or намно́го ста́рше, never «о́чень ста́рше».
title: The comparative: бо́льше, лу́чше and чем

examples.en: You need to get some sleep.

note:
Russian expresses a state or a need with an impersonal sentence: the person who feels it is in the dative, and the word with it ends in «-о», with no subject.

• Мне хо́лодно. - I'm cold.
• Ему́ ску́чно. - He is bored.
• Мне на́до, мне ну́жно. - I need to, I have to.
• Мо́жно. - It's allowed, one may.
• Нельзя́. - It's forbidden, one must not.

Past: Мне бы́ло хо́лодно; future: Мне бу́дет хо́лодно.

Note: нельзя́ usually means «not allowed», not «I am unable to»: Мне нельзя́ кури́ть - I'm not allowed to smoke.
title: Impersonal sentences: мне хо́лодно, мне ну́жно, мо́жно, нельзя́

note:
Russian turns «I like it» around: the person who likes is in the dative, and the thing liked is the subject, so the verb agrees with it.

• Мне нра́вится э́тот го́род. - I like this city.
• Мне нра́вятся э́ти фи́льмы. - I like these movies.
• Ей нра́вился го́род, нра́вилась кни́га, нра́вились фи́льмы - the past tense agrees with the thing liked (she liked the city, the book, the movies).
• Ты мне нра́вишься. - I like you.

Нра́виться is not люби́ть: Я люблю́ кино́ - I love movies (in general, always); Мне нра́вится э́тот фильм - I like this movie (a judgment of one particular thing).
title: Мне нра́вится: the thing liked is the subject

note:
«Let's...» in Russian is дава́й + the «we» form of a perfective verb, or дава́й + the infinitive of an imperfective verb.

• Дава́й пойдём в кино́. - Let's go to the movies.
• Дава́й встре́тимся в пять. - Let's meet at five.
• Дава́й чита́ть. - Let's read.

To several people or politely: дава́йте.

The imperative is formed like this: чита́й, чита́йте; пиши́, пиши́те; иди́, иди́те; -те is added for several people or for the polite «you».
title: The imperative and дава́й(те): «let's»

examples.en: I'll call Mom in the evening.
I thank you for your help.

note:
These Russian verbs take cases that English does not lead you to expect:

• звони́ть + dat. - to call someone: Я позвоню́ ма́ме - I'll call Mom.
• благодари́ть + acc. - to thank someone: Благодарю́ вас - I thank you.
• поздравля́ть + acc. + «с» + instr. - to congratulate someone on something: «Поздравля́ю тебя́ с днём рожде́ния» - Happy birthday to you.

Ждать takes the accusative or the genitive: ждать авто́бус, ждать отве́та (to wait for the bus, to wait for an answer).
title: Verbs with unexpected cases: звони́ть, благодари́ть, поздравля́ть

note:
These verbs take a preposition and a case that you cannot guess from English:

• смея́ться над + instr. - to laugh at someone: Они́ смею́тся над ним.
• жени́ться на + prep. - (of a man) to marry someone: Он жени́лся на ней.
• вы́йти за́муж за + acc. - (of a woman) to marry someone
• ду́мать о + prep. - to think of someone: Я ду́маю о тебе́.
• скуча́ть по + dat. - to miss someone: Я скуча́ю по тебе́ - I miss you.

English «to marry» takes a plain object, but Russian жени́ться and вы́йти за́муж always need their preposition.
title: Verbs with a preposition: смея́ться над, жени́ться на, ду́мать о

related.en: to do (a sport, a subject), to study

note:
Four verbs, four constructions:

• игра́ть в + acc. - to play a game or sport: игра́ть в футбо́л, в ша́хматы
• игра́ть на + prep. - to play an instrument: игра́ть на гита́ре, на пиани́но
• по́льзоваться + instr. - to use: по́льзоваться телефо́ном, интерне́том
• занима́ться + instr. - to do, to study: занима́ться спо́ртом, занима́ться ру́сским

In English these verbs take a plain object (play soccer, play the guitar, use a phone); in Russian the preposition or the case is part of the verb.
title: Игра́ть, по́льзоваться, занима́ться

examples.en: This is a gift for Mom.
I'm going to get some bread.

related.en: for (a reason, a price); (go) to get

note:
English «for» is split into three cases in Russian.

• для + gen. - purpose, benefit: пода́рок для ма́мы (a gift for Mom), ко́мната для госте́й (a room for guests)
• за + acc. - reason, price: спаси́бо за по́мощь (thanks for the help), плати́ть за обе́д (to pay for lunch)
• за + instr. - going to fetch: идти́ за хле́бом (to go get bread), пойти́ за молоко́м (to go get milk)

So «thanks for...» does not use для, and «to go for bread» is за + instr.
title: для and за: «for» whom, «for» what

examples.en: On Saturdays we go to the swimming pool.

note:
Russian по + dat. has several meanings.

• по телефо́ну, по по́чте - by phone, by mail
• по у́лице, по го́роду - along the street, around the city (moving about)
• по понеде́льникам, по вечера́м - on Mondays, in the evenings (always, regularly)
• по-ру́сски - in Russian: говори́ть по-ру́сски

Remember also: по-ру́сски is written with a hyphen, and «по ру́сски» does not exist.
title: The preposition по + dative

examples.en: I did it in an hour.

note:
English «in an hour» is two different things in Russian, and «ago» is a third:

• че́рез + acc. - in (from now): Я приду́ че́рез час - I'll come in an hour.
• назад - ago: Он ушёл час наза́д - He left an hour ago. Наза́д comes after the time expression.
• за + acc. - within, taking: Я сде́лал э́то за час - I did it in an hour (it took an hour).

The trap is «in an hour»: it can be че́рез час (from now) or за час (finished within that time).
title: Time: че́рез, наза́д, за

examples.en: The movie starts at seven o'clock.

note:
English «on», «in» and «at» with a day, a month and an hour take different cases in Russian.

• day - в + acc.: в понеде́льник, в пя́тницу, в суббо́ту
• month - в + prep.: в ма́е, в а́вгусте
• hour - в + acc.: в пять часо́в, в два часа́, в час

Date: a neuter ordinal number + the month in the genitive.
• Сего́дня пе́рвое ма́я. - Today is May 1st.
• Когда́? Пе́рвого ма́я. - When? On May 1st.

No в is used with a date.
title: Days, months, hours, dates

examples.en: This is a very important problem.

note:
English has no grammatical gender, so these nouns are worth learning one by one: their gender often surprises learners.

• пробле́ма, систе́ма, програ́мма - feminine, because they end in -а: ва́жная пробле́ма
• боль - feminine: си́льная боль (strong pain)
• мето́д - masculine
• ко́фе - masculine, does not change: чёрный ко́фе (black coffee)
• пальто́, кино́, метро́, такси́ - neuter, do not change: моё пальто́ (my coat)
title: Nouns with surprising gender

note:
Russian «о» sounds like a clear «о» only in a stressed syllable. In the syllable right before the stress it is read as «а» (as in «father»), and in other unstressed syllables as a very short, weak «а» (as in «sofa»).

• молоко́ - approximately «малако́»
• хорошо́ - «харашо́»
• вода́ - «вада́»

It is always written «о», never «а»: молоко́, not «малоко». So the stress matters: it decides how every «о» in the word is read. This is called «а́канье».
title: Unstressed «о» is read as «а»

note:
Unstressed «е» and «я» before the stressed syllable and at the end of a word are pronounced as a short «и» (as in «bit»), not as a clear «ye» or «ya».

• сестра́ - «систра́»
• язы́к - «изы́к»
• де́вять - «де́вить»
• до́ме (в до́ме) - «до́ми»

Under stress «е» and «я» are clear: нет, мя́со, пять. A clear «е» in сестра́ at once gives a foreigner away.
title: Unstressed «е» and «я» sound like «и»

examples.en: I was at home all day.

note:
«Ы» is a sound between «и» and «у»: say «и» (as in «machine») with the tongue pulled back and the lips not spread into a smile.

• мы - we, вы - you, ты - you (informal)
• быть - to be, бить - to beat
• мы́ло - soap, ми́ло - sweet, cute

The difference in the sound changes the meaning, so you need to hear it.

Spelling rules:
• «ы» is not written at the beginning of a word
• after «г», «к», «х» «и» is written: кни́ги, ру́ки
• after «ж», «ш», «ц» «и» is written, but it is read as «ы»: жизнь, ши́на, цирк
title: The letter ы: a sound English does not have

examples.en: We need a little more salt.

note:
The soft sign «ь» has no sound of its own: it makes the consonant before it soft. «Ль» is like «ly» in «million» and «нь» is like «ny» in «canyon».

• конь - horse
• учи́тель - teacher
• у́голь - coal, but у́гол - corner (no «ь», a hard «л»)

Any other consonant can be soft as well: мать, есть, семь - «т», «с» and «м» are soft, and English has no letter for that.

After «ж», «ш», «ч», «щ» the «ь» does not change the pronunciation, it only shows the feminine gender: ночь, мышь.
title: The soft sign ь

examples.en: We live in the first entrance.
This is a family from Serbia.

note:
«Ъ» is rare: it is written only after a prefix ending in a consonant, before the letters «е», «ё», «ю», «я». It means that the consonant stays hard and that a «y» sound (as in «yes») is heard before the vowel.

• объяви́ть - to announce, read «об-йави́ть»
• подъе́зд - entrance of a building, «под-йе́зд»
• съесть - to eat up, «с-йесть»

The soft sign «ь» works similarly before the same letters, but it also softens the consonant: семья́ - «семйа́», статья́ - «статйа́».
title: The hard sign ъ

note:
The English «y» (as in «yes») is written in two ways in Russian:
• й - after a vowel: мой, май, чай
• я, е, ё, ю - at the start of a word or after a vowel: я (I), есть (there is), моё (my, n.), юг (south)

After a consonant these letters do not add a «y» sound: they only soften the consonant before them: нет is like «nyet».

Russian «ч» is like «ch» in «church»: чай. «Щ» is a long, soft «shch», as in «fresh cheese»: борщ. The English «j» as in «jeans» is written «дж»: джи́нсы.
title: The sound «y» and the letters ч, щ, дж

note:
«Ё» is read as «yo» (as in «yonder») and is always stressed, so it never needs a stress mark.

In books, newspapers and messages the two dots are usually left out and a plain «е» is written. So the stress has to be known:
• все - everyone, всё - everything
• не́бо - sky, нёбо - palate
• лёд - ice, read «lyot»

After a consonant «ё» does not add a «y» sound: it softens the consonant and is read like «о».
title: The letter ё: always stressed, often written as е

examples.en: We looked around the old castle.

note:
Russian stress is free: it can fall on any syllable, it is not shown in normal writing, and it can move between the forms of a word:
• рука́ - ру́ку
• голова́ - го́лову
• го́род - города́ (pl.)

The stress can also change the meaning: за́мок - castle, замо́к - lock; му́ка - torment, мука́ - flour.

A stressed vowel is clear and strong, an unstressed one is weakened (see the notes on «а́канье»). So learn each word with its stress, as the cards show it.
title: Free and mobile stress

note:
At the end of a word a Russian voiced consonant is pronounced voiceless, but it is written as usual.

• хлеб - «хлеп»
• го́род - «го́рат»
• друг - «друк»
• нож - «нош»

The same happens in the middle of a word when a voiced and a voiceless consonant meet: ска́зка - «ска́ска», вокза́л - «вагза́л».

The spelling does not change, only the pronunciation.
title: Voiced consonants at the end of a word

examples.en: I've known him for a long time.

note:
In the endings «-ого» and «-его» of adjectives and pronouns the letter «г» is read as «в». It is written «г», but you hear «v».

• его́ - «ево́»
• но́вого - «но́вово»
• како́го - «каково́»
• ничего́ - «ничево́»
• сего́дня - «сево́дня»

Words without that ending are an exception: мно́го, до́рого, стро́го are read with «г».
title: The letter г is read as в in -ого and -его

note:
In что and что́бы the letters «чт» are read as «шт»: что - «што», что́бы - «што́бы». Что means «what».

It is the same in a few common words:
• коне́чно - «коне́шно», of course
• ску́чно - «ску́шно», boring
• наро́чно - «наро́шно», on purpose

It is not so everywhere: то́чно and ночно́й are read with «ч».
title: How to read что, чтобы and конечно

examples.en: She is Serbian, and he is Russian.

note:
Russian writes foreign names by ear, and it has no letters for the Serbian sounds đ, ć, dž and j, so Serbian names look different.

• Đoković - Джо́кович (đ becomes «дж», -ić becomes «-ич»)
• Jovanović - Йо́ванович
• Beograd - Белгра́д
• Srbija - Се́рбия

Every surname in -ić ends in «-ич» in Russian.

The adjective is се́рбский, a Serbian man is серб, a Serbian woman is се́рбка. The Serbian language is се́рбский язы́к.
title: Serbian names and places in Russian text

examples.ru: [Вы] не подскажете, как пройти на вокзал?
examples.en: Excuse me, could you tell me how to get to the station?

related.en: patronymic (a name made from the father's first name)

note:
Russian has two words for «you»: «ты» for close friends, family and children, and «Вы» for strangers, older people and formal situations. «Вы» is also the plural. In a letter or message to one person «Вы» is written with a capital letter.

The switch to «ты» is made by agreement: Дава́йте на «ты».

Russians have an о́тчество, a middle name made from the father's first name. With «Вы» people usually use the first name and the patronymic: Ива́н Петро́вич, Мари́я Ива́новна. The first name alone means a closer relationship.
title: Ты and Вы, first name and patronymic

examples.en: Hello, I'm calling about the ad.

note:
Greetings depend on «ты» or «Вы»:
• здра́вствуйте - formal, at any time of day (the first «в» is not pronounced)
• приве́т - informal, for both hello and goodbye
• до́брый день, до́брый ве́чер, до́брое у́тро - by the time of day

Goodbyes:
• до свида́ния - formal
• пока́ - informal, like «bye»
• споко́йной но́чи - good night, before going to sleep

Здо́рово! is an informal greeting, but it also means «great».
title: Greetings and goodbyes

examples.en: - Thanks for the help! - You're welcome.

related.en: please; here you are; you're welcome

note:
Пожа́луйста covers several English expressions:
• please - when you ask for something
• here you are - when you hand something over
• you're welcome - as a reply to thanks

Thanks:
• спаси́бо - thank you (from «спаси Бог»)
• благодарю́ - I thank you, formal or in writing

Another reply to thanks: не́ за что - don't mention it.

When you did not hear something and ask «pardon?», you do not say пожа́луйста, but что? or прости́те?
title: Пожалуйста and спасибо

examples.en: - How's the movie? - Not bad, it's watchable.

note:
In conversation ничего́ is often not «nothing» but a mild answer:
• Как дела́? - Ничего́. = Not bad, so-so.
• Извини́те! - Ничего́. = It's all right, never mind.
• Ничего́ стра́шного. = No harm done.
• Ничего́ себе́! = Wow! Look at that! (surprise)

Норма́льно is similar: Как дела́? - Норма́льно. = Fine, OK.
title: Ничего́: not always «nothing»

note:
Дава́й(те) most often means «let's»:
• Дава́й встре́тимся! - Let's meet.
• Ла́дно, дава́й. - Okay, talk to you later (at the end of a conversation).
• Дава́йте - for «Вы» or several people.

It is followed by the «we» form of a perfective verb: дава́й пойдём, дава́й позвони́м.

Дава́й is also the imperative of дава́ть, «to give»: Дава́й де́ньги! - Give me the money! The meaning is clear from the sentence.
title: Давай: «let's» and more

examples.en: Let's go home, it's already late.
Everyone got into the car. - Off we go!

note:
«Let's go» in Russian is пошли́ (on foot) and пое́хали (by vehicle).
• Пошли́ в кино́! - Let's go to the movies.
• Пое́хали! - Off we go! (by car or train; also when something is starting)

Пошли́ is also the imperative of посла́ть (to send) and the past plural of пойти́, so only the context tells them apart.

Пошли́ ему письмо́ - Send him a letter.
Они пошли́ домо́й - They went home.
title: Пошли́ and пое́хали: «let's go»

note:
In conversation Russian often uses diminutives, and not only about children:
• ча́шечка - a little cup
• мину́точку - a moment
• води́чка - a little water
• бу́лочка - a bun

They show politeness, closeness or a small amount: Подожди́те мину́точку - Wait a moment; Нале́й води́чки - Pour me a little water.

In official speech and about serious matters diminutives sound cutesy or ironic.
title: Diminutives in everyday speech

examples.en: I'm busy right now, I'll call you later.

note:
Сейча́с means «now», but also «right away» and «in a moment», depending on the tone.
• Я сейча́с на рабо́те. - I'm at work now.
• Сейча́с приду́! - I'll be right there.
• Сейча́с! - Coming! (when you are called and are still finishing something)

For Russians сейча́с is not a sharp deadline and often means «in a minute». When you mean really at once, say сра́зу or пря́мо сейча́с.
title: Сейча́с: now, right away and in a little while

examples.en: We have lived on this street for a long time.

note:
Abbreviations are written short, but they are read in full:
• т. е. - то е́сть - that is
• т. д. - и так да́лее - and so on
• т. п. - и тому́ подо́бное - and the like
• г. - год (1990 г.) or го́род (г. Москва)
• ул. - у́лица
• руб. - рубль

A space goes inside an abbreviation too: «т. д.», not «т.д.»
title: Common abbreviations in Russian text

examples.en: My apartment is on the fifth floor.
The pharmacy is on the first floor.

note:
Russians count floors as Americans do: when someone says «на пе́рвом этаже́», they mean the ground floor.

• пе́рвый эта́ж - the ground floor (UK ground floor, US first floor)
• второ́й эта́ж - one floor up (UK first floor)
• тре́тий эта́ж - two floors up (UK second floor)

So «я на второ́м этаже́» means «I'm on the second floor» in the American sense.

When you arrange to meet in a building, check how each person counts the floors.
title: Floors: пе́рвый эта́ж is the ground floor

examples.en: Let's sit down for a moment before the trip, and then we'll go.

examples.ru: Перед отъездом мы всегда [сади́мся] на доро́жку.
examples.en: Before leaving we always sit down for a moment.

related.en: to sit down for a moment

note:
Before setting off on a journey, Russians sit down for a few seconds in silence. The custom is called «присе́сть на доро́жку».

• those who are traveling sit down
• then they get up and set off
• it is believed that the trip will go well

Доро́жка is a diminutive of доро́га (road).
title: Sitting down before a journey: присе́сть на доро́жку

examples.en: Please give the guest some slippers.
I brought indoor shoes to the party.

related.en: indoor shoes, a change of shoes (colloq.)

note:
In Russian apartments and houses people do not walk in wearing street shoes.

• the host offers the guest та́почки (slippers)
• someone who does not want to wear slippers brings сме́нную о́бувь (indoor shoes), colloquially сме́нка

At the door you will hear something like «Проходи́те, вот та́почки» (Come in, here are the slippers).
title: Visiting: та́почки and сме́нка

examples.en: Let's drink to the birthday boy's health!

note:
Russians drink «to» someone or something with за + acc.:

• «Вы́пьем за здоро́вье!» - Let's drink to our health!
• «За тебя́!» - To you!
• «За роди́телей!» - To the parents!

Before a toast the host checks the glasses: «У всех нали́то?» - Does everyone have a drink?

A toast is often a little story, not just one sentence.
title: A toast: пить за + accusative

examples.en: Happy New Year in advance! Wishing you health and happiness!

note:
Before midnight on December 31 Russians say «С наступа́ющим!» (short for «с наступа́ющим Но́вым го́дом»). When the clock strikes twelve, they say «С Но́вым го́дом!».

• «С наступа́ющим!» - Happy New Year (before it arrives)
• «С Но́вым го́дом!» - Happy New Year

The same pattern, «с» + instr., works for every holiday: «С днём рожде́ния!» (Happy birthday!), «С Рождество́м!» (Merry Christmas!)
title: Greetings before a holiday: с наступа́ющим

examples.ru: В ночь на четырнадцатое мы отмечаем [Ста́рый Но́вый год].
examples.en: On the night of the 13th to the 14th we celebrate the Old New Year.

note:
Ста́рый Но́вый год is celebrated on the night of January 13 to 14, by the Julian calendar.

• in Russia it is an ordinary working day, so only some people celebrate it
• the main holiday is Но́вый год on January 1, and Рождество́ (Christmas) is on January 7

The name is written with a capital letter in every word: «Ста́рый Но́вый год».
title: Ста́рый Но́вый год: the Old New Year

examples.ru: [День защи́тника Оте́чества] у нас всегда отмечают дома.
examples.en: We always celebrate Defender of the Fatherland Day at home.

note:
February 23 is a day off in Russia: День защи́тника Оте́чества (Defender of the Fatherland Day).

• from 1949 it was called День Сове́тской а́рмии и Вое́нно-морско́го фло́та (Soviet Army and Navy Day)
• today it is the "men's holiday": all men are congratulated, from boys to grandfathers
• the women's counterpart is 8 ма́рта (March 8)

«Поздравля́ю с днём защи́тника Оте́чества!» - Happy Defender of the Fatherland Day!
title: February 23: День защи́тника Оте́чества

examples.ru: Не будь такой [пла́ксой], всё будет хорошо.
examples.en: Don't be such a crybaby, everything will be fine.

note:
Some nouns in «-а» and «-я» can refer to a man or a woman. This is called «common gender».

The adjective, pronoun and verb show the gender:
• Он тако́й пла́кса - He is such a crybaby
• Она́ така́я пла́кса - She is such a crybaby

Likewise: зану́да (nitpicker), со́ня (sleepyhead), сирота́ (orphan).
title: Common gender: пла́кса, со́ня, зану́да

examples.en: You learn from mistakes, don't be afraid to make them.

note:
«На оши́бках у́чатся» is a Russian proverb: «you learn from your mistakes».

The verb is in the 3rd person plural, with no subject. This is how Russian says «someone», «they» or «people in general»:
• «Говоря́т, зимо́й бу́дет хо́лодно» - They say it will be cold in winter
• «Здесь не ку́рят» - There is no smoking here
• «У нас так де́лают» - That's how we do it
title: На оши́бках у́чатся and the indefinite subject

examples.ru: Отец шахматист, и сын выиграл турнир. [Я́блоко от я́блони недалеко́ па́дает].
examples.en: The father is a chess player, and the son won a tournament. The apple doesn't fall far from the tree.

note:
«Я́блоко от я́блони недалеко́ па́дает» means that a child resembles the parents. It is the Russian «the apple doesn't fall far from the tree».

It is said when a child inherits a talent or a habit of the parents, usually with a smile.

After the preposition от the noun goes into the genitive: от я́блони.
title: A proverb about an apple: я́блоко от я́блони

examples.en: This bag is beyond my budget.

examples.ru: Он за словом в [карма́н] не лезет.
examples.en: He's never at a loss for words.

note:
Карма́н (pocket) appears in several common sayings:

• «Держи́ карма́н ши́ре!» - Don't count on it, you wish (ironic; literally: hold your pocket wider)
• «Э́то мне не по карма́ну» - I can't afford that
• «Он за сло́вом в карма́н не ле́зет» - He always has an answer, he is never at a loss for words
title: Pocket in sayings: карма́н

examples.en: We have the exam period in January.

examples.ru: Я потерял [зачётку], теперь надо делать новую.
examples.en: I lost my grade book, now I have to get a new one.

note:
Words that confuse you when you enroll in a Russian university:

• се́ссия - the exam period (not a «session» of a meeting)
• экза́мен - an exam, зачёт - a pass/fail test without a grade
• зачётка - the grade book, a small booklet where grades are recorded
• бакалавриа́т and магистрату́ра - bachelor's and master's studies
• аспиранту́ра - doctoral studies

Students' Day is January 25: Татья́нин день.
title: Student life: се́ссия, зачётка

examples.ru: На завтрак у нас [ка́ша] с молоком.
examples.en: For breakfast we have porridge with milk.

related.en: porridge, a thick dish of cooked grain

note:
Ка́ша is a thick dish of boiled grain or rice: гре́чневая (buckwheat), овся́ная (oatmeal), ма́нная (semolina), ри́совая (rice).

• ри́совая ка́ша на молоке́ - rice cooked in milk, a bit like a thin rice pudding
• in Russia ка́ша is eaten for breakfast or as a snack, not as a dessert
title: Ка́ша: breakfast, not dessert

examples.ru: Мы с детьми наряжаем [ёлку] за неделю до праздника.
examples.en: The kids and I decorate the New Year tree a week before the holiday.
Children wait for presents from Grandfather Frost.

note:
New Year is the main winter holiday in Russia, with a tree and presents. Рождество́ (Christmas) comes only on January 7.

• ёлка - the fir tree; наряжа́ть ёлку - to decorate the tree
• ёлочные игру́шки - tree ornaments
• Дед Моро́з - Grandfather Frost
• мишура́ - tinsel; гирля́нда - string lights
• фейерве́рк - fireworks; шампа́нское - champagne (sparkling wine)
title: New Year words: ёлка, Дед Моро́з, мишура́
